abstract.p: Intelligent supplier selection is an important component of industrial supply chain management, where economic performance, environmental sustainability, social responsibility, and operational reliability must be considered under uncertain and often conflicting information. Although machine learning supports data-driven supplier evaluation, integrating predictive explanations with uncertainty-aware decision models remains a challenge. This study investigates an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI)-based framework for intelligent supplier selection by combining gradient boosting, Shapley value analysis, and multi-polar interval-valued neutrosophic hypersoft sets ($m$-Polar IVNHSS). A class of concave generator functions was developed to construct weighted distance and similarity measures using sine, exponential, hyperbolic-tangent, and hybrid functions. The proposed measures were shown to satisfy the metric axioms under positive weights, while a tangent-based measure was demonstrated to violate the triangle inequality. Shapley values derived from a gradient-boosting classifier were used to select relevant supplier sub-attributes, determine criterion weights, and support interpretable candidate screening. The framework was evaluated through three simulated industrial supplier selection cases involving electric-vehicle battery cells, organic-cotton fabric, and compostable packaging. Validation on 150 held-out suppliers per case yielded area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values of 0.802, 0.630, and 0.837 for the hybrid similarity measure. Ablation experiments showed that data-driven sub-attribute selection contributed more to predictive discrimination than weight adjustment, while sensitivity analysis identified the hybrid generator as the most stable option among the proposed parameterized measures. These findings indicate that explainable machine learning and uncertainty-aware similarity measures can be integrated into a transparent industrial decision framework. The proposed approach provides a mathematically grounded basis for interpretable supplier ranking and supports the development of intelligent procurement decision systems, although validation using real industrial data remains necessary.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Supplier selection plays an important role in industrial supply chain management, as the reliability, quality and sustainability of external suppliers directly affect manufacturing performance and business continuity. Industrial enterprises must evaluate suppliers against several competing criteria, including purchasing costs, environmental performance, labour practices and operational reliability. These decisions become particularly difficult when information is incomplete, evaluation criteria are interdependent, and different departments hold conflicting assessments [1]. The increasing availability of industrial and supplier-related data has created opportunities to support procurement decisions through artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning and intelligent decision-support systems. Recent studies have highlighted the growing role of these technologies in supply chain management, while also identifying substantial challenges in translating analytical capabilities into reliable procurement decisions [2], [3], [4].

Intelligent supplier selection involves more than predicting whether a supplier will perform satisfactorily. Procurement managers must understand which supplier characteristics influence the results, how evaluation criteria are weighted and whether the resulting rankings remain dependable under uncertain conditions. Existing research on AI-supported procurement has demonstrated the potential of machine learning to analyse supplier information and support purchasing activities [5]. Hybrid approaches combining machine learning with multi-criteria decision-making have also been developed to retain interpretable decision procedures while using historical data to identify relevant supplier characteristics [6]. Nevertheless, industrial decision systems must accommodate both uncertainty in supplier assessments and the need for explanations that can be examined by procurement specialists and other stakeholders. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has therefore become an important consideration in the development of data-driven supply chain decision systems [7].

Uncertainty modelling provides another essential component of intelligent industrial decision-making. Conventional numerical assessments may not adequately represent incomplete evidence, conflicting opinions or uncertainty concerning future supplier performance. Fuzzy sets were introduced to represent graded membership rather than strictly binary classifications [8], while intuitionistic fuzzy sets incorporated membership and non-membership degrees [9]. Neutrosophic sets subsequently introduced an additional indeterminacy component, allowing truth, indeterminacy and falsity to be represented independently [10]. Interval-valued neutrosophic sets further allow these assessments to be expressed as ranges rather than precise numerical values [11]. Developments in soft set theory [12], neutrosophic soft sets [13], interval-valued extensions [14] and hypersoft sets [15] have provided increasingly flexible representations of multi-attribute decision problems.

sec.title: 2.1. Neutrosophic and hypersoft structures for uncertain decision-making
sec.p: The representation of uncertain and incomplete information has received considerable attention in multi-criteria decision-making. Fuzzy set theory provides the basis for expressing partial membership [8], while intuitionistic fuzzy sets distinguish membership from non-membership [9]. Neutrosophic sets extend these concepts by introducing truth, indeterminacy and falsity as separate components [10]. Their interval-valued extension allows decision makers to represent assessments using lower and upper bounds, making it possible to describe imprecise evidence without assigning a single numerical value [11].

Soft set theory provides a complementary approach to parameter-based uncertainty modelling [12]. Neutrosophic soft sets combine parameterisation with the three neutrosophic components [13], and interval-valued neutrosophic soft sets further accommodate assessments expressed as intervals [14]. Hypersoft sets extend conventional soft sets by replacing individual parameters with combinations of sub-attribute values [15]. This distinction is important in supplier evaluation, where broad criteria such as environmental performance or operational reliability consist of several measurable characteristics that may influence a purchasing decision differently.

These structures are relevant to industrial procurement because information is rarely uniform across departments or evaluation periods. A procurement unit may have relatively precise cost information but limited knowledge of a supplier’s environmental practices, whereas a sustainability department may have access to more detailed environmental assessments. Representing such differences through separate poles and interval-valued evaluations allows the decision model to retain information that would otherwise be lost through premature aggregation.

Nevertheless, uncertainty representation alone does not determine how alternatives should be compared. A practical intelligent decision system also requires suitable operators for measuring differences between evaluations and translating those differences into supplier rankings. The mathematical properties of such operators are therefore central to the reliability of the resulting decision procedure.

sec.title: 2.2. Distance and similarity measures in neutrosophic decision models
sec.p: Distance and similarity measures provide a mathematical basis for comparing uncertain assessments. In supplier selection, these measures are commonly used to evaluate how closely each supplier approaches an ideal profile or how strongly its characteristics differ from those of competing alternatives. The general principle of ranking alternatives according to their distances from ideal solutions is well established in multi-attribute decision-making [29].

Within neutrosophic modelling, Broumi and Smarandache [18] investigated similarity measures for neutrosophic sets, while Ye [19] developed vector-based similarity measures for simplified neutrosophic information. Mondal and Pramanik [20] introduced a tangent similarity measure, which was subsequently considered in the context of neutrosophic hypersoft structures by Saqlain et al. [21]. These contributions established several ways of comparing evaluations containing truth, indeterminacy and falsity information.

Despite these contributions, the mathematical design of similarity-based models remains an important issue. Existing measures commonly employ specific functional forms, including absolute differences, Euclidean distances, vector similarity and trigonometric transformations. Their use in a particular decision problem does not automatically establish that every transformation preserves the properties of a metric. In particular, non-negativity, symmetry, identity of indiscernibles and the triangle inequality must be considered when a function is intended to represent a metric distance.

This distinction matters in industrial intelligent decision systems. A ranking procedure based solely on distance from an ideal profile may produce an ordering even when the underlying comparison function does not satisfy all metric properties. However, applications involving clustering, agreement analysis or repeated comparisons between supplier profiles may require stronger mathematical consistency. Consequently, identifying a general class of admissible transformations is more useful than introducing additional functional forms without a common theoretical basis.

The present study addresses this issue through concave generator functions. Rather than replacing established similarity-based decision models, it investigates conditions under which weighted transformations of interval endpoint differences produce mathematically valid distance measures. The proposed construction also allows different responses to small and large deviations from an ideal supplier profile. This provides a theoretical basis for selecting similarity functions in uncertainty-aware industrial decision applications.

sec.title: 2.3. Intelligent supplier selection and explainable artificial intelligence
sec.p: Sustainable supplier selection has traditionally been addressed through multi-criteria decision-making, where alternatives are assessed according to economic, environmental and social criteria. Reviews of green supplier evaluation have documented the extensive use of weighting methods, fuzzy approaches and distance-based ranking procedures [1]. More recent research has examined how AI, supply chain resilience and sustainability considerations can be incorporated into supplier selection models [30].

The development of Industry 4.0 and data-driven procurement has encouraged the use of machine learning to analyse historical supplier information. Studies of AI adoption in purchasing and supply management indicate that intelligent analytical tools can support supplier evaluation, procurement planning and other purchasing activities, although implementation remains uneven across organisations [3], [5]. The systematic review by Gidiagba et al. [4] further examined machine learning applications in sustainable supplier selection, including their roles in criteria identification, evaluation and ranking. Recent research has also applied supervised machine learning to supplier performance evaluation and risk profiling, demonstrating its relevance to data-driven supply chain decision-making [31].

A central issue in these applications is the interpretability of machine learning predictions. Models trained on supplier performance data may identify complex relationships between input characteristics and historical outcomes, but procurement managers still need explanations that can be examined in relation to organisational priorities. This is particularly important where purchasing decisions involve environmental compliance, labour practices or long-term operational commitments. Research on XAI in supply chain management has identified limited explainability as a significant obstacle to the wider adoption of intelligent analytical methods [7].

Shapley-value analysis provides one approach to explaining predictive models. Originally introduced in cooperative game theory [22], Shapley values were subsequently adapted to explain individual machine learning predictions [23]. The interventional formulation considered by Janzing et al. [24] provides a framework for examining feature contributions under a specified intervention-based value function. Gradient boosting [25] offers a suitable predictive model for structured supplier data, while Shapley attribution allows the contribution of individual supplier characteristics to be examined at both local and global levels.

The integration of machine learning and multi-criteria decision-making has also been investigated directly. Abdulla and Baryannis [6] proposed an explainable supplier selection framework combining data-driven learning with an interpretable decision procedure. Their study demonstrated the relevance of retaining transparent multi-criteria ranking while using machine learning to manage the complexity of supplier information. Recent research has also combined machine learning with multi-criteria evaluation and optimisation to support supplier selection and order allocation under uncertainty [32].

These studies show that combining predictive learning with interpretable multi-criteria decision-making is an established research direction. The remaining question is how feature attribution can be incorporated into a decision structure that also represents multiple sources of interval-valued uncertainty. The present study addresses this question by using Shapley values to select one relevant sub-attribute from each evaluation category, derive criterion weights and support candidate screening. The selected attributes are subsequently evaluated within the $m$-Polar IVNHSS framework.

An important distinction is that Shapley values are used here as measures of predictive feature contribution rather than as direct evidence of causal influence. The framework therefore provides an interpretable means of structuring supplier evaluations from historical performance patterns, while the mathematical distance measures address uncertainty in the subsequent ranking process.

sec.title: 2.4. Research gaps and positioning of the present study
sec.p: The preceding literature indicates that uncertainty modelling, similarity-based decision-making and explainable machine learning have developed into substantial research areas. Their combination is particularly relevant to intelligent industrial procurement, where data-driven recommendations must remain understandable and account for uncertain assessments. sec.title: 4. Proposed distance and similarity measures
sec.p: Reliable supplier ranking requires a consistent means of comparing uncertain assessments with an ideal supplier profile. Conventional distance functions provide useful reference measures, but different transformations of interval discrepancies may respond differently to small and large deviations. This section introduces a class of concave generators for constructing weighted distances and corresponding similarity measures on $m$-Polar IVNHSS. The construction is intended to provide mathematical consistency while allowing the decision maker to adjust sensitivity to deviations from the ideal.

sec.title: 5. Explainable artificial intelligence-based intelligent supplier decision framework
sec.p: The proposed framework integrates predictive learning, feature attribution and uncertainty-aware similarity measures to support intelligent supplier selection. Industrial procurement decisions often involve numerous evaluation criteria, but not all sub-attributes contribute equally to supplier performance. Moreover, different departments or information sources may provide assessments with varying degrees of uncertainty. The framework addresses these issues through two connected stages: data-driven decision structuring and interval-valued supplier ranking.

In the first stage, a gradient-boosting classifier was used to analyse historical supplier performance patterns. Shapley-value explanations were then employed to identify relevant sub-attributes, derive criterion weights and support candidate screening. In the second stage, the selected suppliers were represented using $m$-Polar IVNHSS evaluations and ranked according to the similarity measures developed in Section 4. The resulting procedure combines predictive information with explicit uncertainty representation, while allowing decision makers to examine and revise the choices suggested by the model.

sec.title: 6. Experimental design and industrial case studies
6.1. Common experimental design
sec.p: Three simulated industrial supplier selection cases were considered to examine the proposed framework under different sources of uncertainty. The cases involved electric-vehicle battery cells (case study1) (CS1), organic-cotton fabric (CS2), and compostable packaging (CS3). Although the industrial settings differed, the same predictive modelling and uncertainty-aware ranking procedures were applied throughout.

Each case contained four evaluation categories: Economic, Environmental, Social, and Operational. Three candidate sub-attributes were included in each category, giving a total of 12 input features. The simulated historical dataset comprised 600 supplier engagements with binary success outcomes. Eight candidate suppliers were considered in each case, and the five candidates with the highest predicted success probabilities were retained for detailed assessment.

Each case incorporated three poles, representing different sources or dimensions of uncertainty. In CS1, the poles corresponded to the Procurement Department, Sustainability Office, and Operations Unit. In CS2, they represented planning horizons of one year, three years, and at least five years. In CS3, they represented third-party audits, supplier self-assessments, and on-site inspections.

All evaluation criteria were oriented so that larger values indicated more favourable performance. Cost-type attributes were transformed using

A gradient-boosting classifier was employed to estimate supplier success probabilities [25]. The model contained 250 trees with a maximum depth of 3, a learning rate of 0.05, and a subsampling rate of 0.80. Unless otherwise stated, the generator parameter was set to

The simulated supplier records were generated using a fixed, seeded process incorporating nonlinear relationships and an interaction between environmental and social characteristics. The use of synthetic data allowed the proposed method to be examined under controlled conditions without relying on confidential procurement records.

Shapley-value analysis was used to identify one sub-attribute from each evaluation category and derive the corresponding criterion weights. The retained suppliers were subsequently evaluated using $m$-Polar IVNHSS representations and ranked according to similarity to the ideal supplier profile. sec.title: 6.2. Case study 1: electric-vehicle battery cell suppliers
sec.p: The first case examined the selection of a lithium-ion battery cell supplier for an automotive manufacturer. Supplier evaluation in this setting involves purchasing costs, environmental impacts, labour practices and delivery reliability. The three poles represented the Procurement Department, Sustainability Office and Operations Unit, allowing differences between organisational perspectives to be retained in the assessment.

The gradient-boosting classifier achieved a cross-validated area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.792 and an accuracy of 0.703, with a baseline success rate of 0.500. Shapley-value analysis identified four sub-attributes—Unit cost, Carbon intensity, Labour-rights audit score, and Delivery reliability—which together accounted for 62.6% of the total global feature importance (as shown in Figure 3).

Labour-rights audit score received the greatest relative weight among the selected criteria. This result reflected its predictive contribution in the simulated dataset and should not be interpreted as evidence that labour practices necessarily dominate supplier performance in actual battery manufacturing.

The initial screening excluded suppliers B2, B4 and B5, whose predicted success probabilities were 0.217, 0.151 and 0.312, respectively. The local Shapley explanations identified Delivery reliability as the largest negative contributor for suppliers B2 and B5, while Unit cost contributed most negatively to the prediction for B4. Such explanations illustrate how an intelligent procurement system can provide information about the characteristics associated with an unfavourable prediction, rather than reporting a score alone.

The five retained suppliers were subsequently evaluated using interval-valued truth, indeterminacy, and falsity assessments from the three decision-making units. These assessments were used to construct the $m$-Polar IVNHSS supplier profiles for similarity-based ranking. The Sustainability Office produced the widest intervals because its information about costs and delivery was less direct, whereas the Operations Unit produced the narrowest intervals. These differences were reflected in the pole weights shown in Figure 3.

The three poles represented planning horizons of one year, three years and at least five years. Longer planning horizons were assigned wider evaluation intervals to represent greater uncertainty about future supplier performance.

sec.title: 6.5. Cross-case comparison

Across the three simulated cases, all four proposed generators identified the same highest-ranked supplier at

The tangent and cosine reference measures reproduced the Hamming ordering in CS1 and CS2, while differences appeared among closely ranked suppliers in CS3. The sine, hyperbolic-tangent, and hybrid generators were reported to produce wider score ranges than Hamming. These findings indicate that nonlinear transformations affect the numerical separation of supplier profiles, although greater score separation does not necessarily imply higher predictive accuracy. The predictive discrimination of the resulting similarity scores is examined in Section 7.

sec.title: 7. Comparative evaluation and validation
sec.p: The practical value of an intelligent supplier ranking method depends on whether its scores provide useful information about subsequent supplier performance. To examine this question, the proposed similarity measures were evaluated using held-out observations generated independently from the same simulation process as the training data.

For each case, 150 additional suppliers were generated. These observations were not used to train the classifier, calculate the Shapley attributions or construct the original candidate evaluation matrices. Each held-out supplier was represented using an $m$-Polar IVNHSS evaluation consistent with the corresponding case structure. Similarity to the ideal supplier profile was then calculated using the selected sub-attributes and XAI-derived weights.

The AUC was used to assess how well each scoring rule distinguished successful from unsuccessful supplier outcomes. Figure 4 compares the AUC results of the proposed similarity measures, reference methods, and two ablation configurations: the hybrid measure with equal criterion weights and the hybrid measure using the least important sub-attributes.

caption.title: AUC comparison of the proposed similarity measures, reference measures and ablation configurations using 150 held-out suppliers per simulated case

sec.p: The hybrid similarity measure achieved AUC values of 0.802, 0.630 and 0.837 in CS1, CS2 and CS3, respectively. The corresponding values for the gradient-boosting classifier were 0.811, 0.710 and 0.848. The differences between the hybrid similarity measure and the classifier were therefore 0.009, 0.080 and 0.011 across the three cases. The hybrid measure approached the classifier’s discrimination performance in CS1 and CS3, although the difference was more pronounced in CS2. These results are notable because the similarity-based decision model used only four selected sub-attributes rather than the complete set of twelve candidate features.

Across the proposed generators, the differences from Hamming did not exceed 0.02 AUC, and no generator consistently achieved higher predictive discrimination. The results therefore do not support a general claim that nonlinear generators improve prediction accuracy. Their principal contribution lies instead in the mathematical properties established in Section 4 and the ability to adjust the response to endpoint discrepancies.

Two ablation experiments were conducted to identify the contributions of feature selection and criterion weighting. In the first, the hybrid similarity measure was evaluated using equal attribute weights. In the second, the selected sub-attributes were replaced with the least important sub-attributes identified by the predictive model.

Replacing the selected tuple with the least important features reduced the AUC to 0.516, 0.509 and 0.688 in CS1–CS3, respectively. The first two values were close to random discrimination. In contrast, replacing the XAI-derived weights with equal weights changed the AUC by no more than approximately 0.02.

These findings indicate that the choice of sub-attributes had a substantially greater influence on discrimination performance than their relative weighting in the simulated cases. The Shapley-based selection procedure was therefore the main empirical contributor to the performance of the resulting similarity scores.

The classifier achieved cross-validated AUC values of 0.792, 0.682, and 0.766 in CS1–CS3, respectively. The comparatively weaker discrimination in CS2 suggests that closely ranked supplier characteristics should be reviewed carefully before making a final decision.

The validation results indicate that the similarity-based decision model retained useful discriminatory information after reducing the original feature set from twelve to four selected sub-attributes.

Nevertheless, the held-out observations were generated from the same underlying process as the training data. The reported AUC values therefore provide evidence of internal validation under controlled conditions, rather than independent confirmation of the framework’s effectiveness in operational industrial procurement. Further evaluation using real supplier records would be necessary to establish its practical generalisability.

sec.title: 8. Robustness and sensitivity analysis
sec.p: Industrial supplier rankings may be affected by modelling choices, estimated criterion weights and the uncertainty associated with different information sources. Sensitivity analysis was therefore conducted to examine whether the proposed recommendations remained consistent under variations in these factors.
Four sources of variation were examined using the hybrid generator as the reference measure: the generator parameter, criterion weights, pole weights, and removal of individual evaluation criteria.

sec.title: 8.2. Sensitivity to attribute weights
sec.p: The XAI-derived criterion weights represent estimates of predictive importance and may vary with the training data. To examine their influence, 2,000 alternative weight vectors were generated from a Dirichlet distribution centred on the original weights, with a concentration parameter of 40.
The resulting coefficient of variation was approximately 15%–20% per weight. Each sampled vector was used to recalculate the supplier rankings.

In CS2, F6 and F4 retained the first and second positions in every simulation. CS1 showed greater sensitivity: B1 ranked first in 68% of the simulations, while B3 ranked first in 30%. Thus, the two leading suppliers were generally stable as a group, although their relative ordering was less certain. B7 remained last in 97% of the simulations.
In CS3, P4 retained first place in 95% of the simulations, while P1 and P2 frequently exchanged the second and third positions.

The results show that the stability of supplier rankings depends on the separation between competing alternatives. Small differences in similarity scores may lead to changes in rank when the criterion weights are perturbed, even when the overall group of preferred suppliers remains similar.
For intelligent procurement systems, such information provides a basis for distinguishing relatively stable recommendations from decisions that require further examination.

sec.title: 8.3. Sensitivity to pole weights
sec.p: Pole weights determine the relative influence of organisational units, planning horizons or evidence sources in the $m$-Polar IVNHSS assessment.

To investigate this effect, supplier rankings were recalculated under equal pole weights and three additional scenarios in which one pole received a weight of 0.70 and the remaining two received 0.15 each.

The CS2 ranking remained unchanged across the examined scenarios. In CS1, B6 and B8 exchanged positions when either the Procurement Department or Sustainability Office received the dominant weight. In CS3, P1 and P2 exchanged positions only when the third-party audit received the greatest weight.
The highest-ranked supplier remained unchanged in all three cases.

These findings indicate that the relative importance assigned to information sources can influence closely ranked suppliers without necessarily altering the leading recommendation. They also illustrate the value of retaining separate pole assessments rather than immediately combining all available information into a single evaluation.

sec.title: 8.4. Sensitivity to criterion removal
sec.p: The final analysis examined the effect of removing individual evaluation criteria. Each criterion was assigned a weight of zero in turn, and the remaining weights were renormalised before recalculating the rankings.
This intervention produced more substantial changes than moderate weight perturbations.

In CS1, removing the Labour-rights audit score criterion moved B8 from fourth to first place and B1 from first to fourth. The leading recommendation in this case therefore depended strongly on the inclusion of the social criterion. Removing Delivery reliability caused only B1 and B3 to exchange the two highest positions.

In CS2, removing Chemical compliance altered some lower-ranked positions, while the leading suppliers remained unchanged. In CS3, P4 ranked either first or second under every criterion-removal scenario.

These results indicate that ranking stability under moderate weight changes does not necessarily imply robustness to the removal of an influential criterion. For industrial supplier evaluation, this distinction is important because the exclusion of environmental, social or operational characteristics may substantially alter the preferred alternative.

Taken together, the sensitivity analyses show that the proposed framework provides more than a single supplier ranking. It allows decision makers to examine how the recommendations depend on mathematical parameters, data-derived weights, information sources and the inclusion of individual criteria.

The results also reinforce the importance of interpreting small differences in similarity scores cautiously. Stable rankings offer stronger support for a recommendation, whereas unstable rankings identify cases in which additional evidence or managerial review may be appropriate.

sec.title: 9. Discussion and industrial implications
sec.p: The proposed framework integrates explainable machine learning with uncertainty-aware similarity measures to support intelligent supplier selection. The findings provide insights into the mathematical properties of supplier comparison methods, the contribution of data-driven feature selection, and the robustness of decisions made under uncertain information.

sec.title: 9.1. Mathematical contribution and decision consistency
sec.p: The principal theoretical contribution is the construction of a class of distance and similarity measures based on concave generator functions. Previous research has developed individual distance and similarity measures for neutrosophic and $m$-Polar interval-valued hypersoft structures [17], [18], [19], [20], [21]. The present study extends this work by identifying general conditions under which transformed endpoint discrepancies satisfy the metric axioms.

The proposed construction provides a common mathematical basis for selecting admissible generators rather than examining each functional form independently. The analysis also demonstrates that a particular convex tangent transformation fails to satisfy the triangle inequality when used in the proposed distance formulation.

These properties are relevant to industrial decision systems that involve repeated comparisons between uncertain supplier profiles. Although the proposed generators produced similar predictive discrimination in the simulated cases, their mathematical properties remain important when distance measures are used for clustering, comparison, or consensus analysis.

The sensitivity parameter provides additional flexibility by controlling how different deviations from an ideal supplier profile contribute to the distance. However, the experimental results do not establish that increasing sensitivity necessarily improves predictive accuracy or ranking stability.

sec.title: 9.2. Explainable artificial intelligence and intelligent supplier evaluation
sec.p: The most important empirical finding concerns the selection of evaluation sub-attributes. The ablation experiments showed that replacing Shapley-selected features with the least important features substantially reduced predictive discrimination, whereas assigning equal weights to the selected features had a comparatively small effect.

This suggests that selecting informative characteristics was more consequential than refining their weights under the examined simulation conditions. The finding highlights the role of data-driven feature selection in structuring intelligent supplier evaluation.

The integration of gradient boosting and Shapley attribution also provides explanations at two levels. Global attributions identify the characteristics retained for detailed assessment, while local explanations indicate which factors contribute positively or negatively to individual supplier predictions.

Nevertheless, Shapley values describe the behaviour of the fitted predictive model and should not be interpreted as causal effects. The derived criteria and weights therefore provide analytical support for procurement decisions rather than replacing organisational priorities or expert judgement.

sec.title: 9.3. Representation of multiple sources of uncertainty
sec.p: The $m$-Polar structure permits different assessment perspectives to be represented without immediately combining them into a single score. The three cases demonstrate its use for organisational departments, planning horizons, and evidence sources.

In CS1, the poles represented assessments from procurement, sustainability, and operations personnel. In CS2, interval widths reflected uncertainty associated with different planning horizons. In CS3, separate poles represented third-party audits, supplier self-assessments, and on-site inspections.

This flexibility is relevant to industrial procurement, where information may vary considerably across organisational functions and external sources. Interval-valued evaluations retain these differences during supplier comparison.

However, narrower intervals do not necessarily indicate more reliable information. The reciprocal-width weighting rule adopted in this study reflects an assumption about assessment precision, and its suitability depends on how the intervals are constructed. Source credibility and assessment uncertainty should therefore be examined separately when applying the framework.

sec.title: 9.4. Implications for industrial decision support
sec.p: The results have three implications for intelligent procurement systems.

First, predictive learning and uncertainty-aware ranking can perform complementary functions. Machine learning identifies informative supplier characteristics and screens candidates, while similarity measures support the subsequent comparison of retained suppliers under uncertain assessments.

Second, the framework provides interpretable information at different decision stages. Shapley attributions explain the predictive model, whereas similarity scores and sensitivity analyses help decision makers understand how criterion weights, information sources, and generator choices affect supplier rankings.

Third, ranking stability should be considered alongside similarity scores. Closely ranked suppliers may exchange positions when modelling assumptions change. A small numerical advantage should therefore not be treated as sufficient evidence for a definitive procurement decision.

These findings support the design of more transparent industrial decision-support procedures. Nevertheless, the present results demonstrate the framework’s behaviour under controlled simulation conditions rather than its effectiveness in an operational procurement environment.

sec.title: 9.5. Limitations and future research
sec.p: The main limitation is the reliance on simulated supplier records. Although the simulation allowed controlled evaluation of nonlinear relationships and uncertainty, the reported AUC values do not establish predictive performance in real industrial settings. Independent validation using actual supplier records remains necessary.

A second limitation concerns the use of predictive feature importance for sub-attribute selection and weighting. Shapley attributions may vary with feature correlations, model specification, and background data. The weaker predictive performance observed in CS2 illustrates the need for caution when interpreting closely ranked characteristics.

The selection of one sub-attribute per evaluation category also reduces the information retained by the decision model. Future studies could investigate procedures that allow several relevant sub-attributes to be included within each category.
In addition, exact enumeration of Shapley coalitions becomes computationally expensive as the feature dimension increases. Larger industrial datasets may require more scalable attribution methods.

Finally, the current framework assumes monotonic preference directions after transforming cost-type criteria. Target-type attributes, such as preferred delivery windows, require further methodological development. Future research should also examine source reliability, correlated evaluation attributes, and uncertainty in the estimated criterion weights.

sec.title: 10. Conclusions
sec.p: This study developed an explainable AI-based intelligent decision framework for sustainable supplier selection under uncertainty. The framework integrated gradient-boosting prediction, Shapley-value attribution, and $m$-Polar interval-valued neutrosophic hypersoft evaluations to support data-driven feature selection and uncertainty-aware supplier ranking.

A class of concave generator functions was introduced to construct weighted distance and similarity measures satisfying defined mathematical properties. Four nonlinear generators were examined, and the theoretical analysis established conditions for metric consistency while identifying a triangle-inequality violation associated with a specific tangent transformation.

The framework was evaluated using three simulated industrial supplier selection cases involving electric-vehicle battery cells, organic-cotton fabric, and compostable packaging. The hybrid similarity measure achieved AUC values of 0.802, 0.630, and 0.837 on 150 held-out suppliers per case. Ablation experiments indicated that sub-attribute selection contributed more to predictive discrimination than criterion-weight adjustment. Sensitivity analysis further showed that the hybrid generator provided relatively stable rankings under the examined parameter settings, although some closely ranked suppliers remained sensitive to modelling choices.

The findings indicate that explainable machine learning and uncertainty-aware similarity measures can be combined to support transparent industrial supplier evaluation. The proposed framework provides a mathematical basis for interpretable ranking and allows decision makers to examine the stability of recommendations under different assumptions.
As the experiments were based on simulated data, further validation using real industrial procurement records is required before practical effectiveness can be established.
